title: Riemann sums & trapezium rule
examples: When should I use the trapezium rule instead of rectangles?
Does the width of the strips affect the accuracy?
How does the number of strips change the result?

explain.say: Today we learn to estimate area using shapes. We look at rectangles and trapezoids.
First we use rectangles called Riemann sums. We pick a point in an interval. We use the height at that point.

items: Pick a point in an interval
Use the height at that point

explain.say: If the function is increasing, the right endpoint gives an overestimate. The left endpoint gives an underestimate.
Next we use the trapezium rule. We connect the endpoints with a straight line. This forms a trapezoid.

items: Connect endpoints with a straight line

explain.say: The area of one trapezoid is an average of the heights times the width. We add these up for the total area.

items: Add these up for total area

faq.q: What is the difference between the trapezium rule and rectangles?
faq.a: Rectangles use only the height at one point. The trapezium rule connects the two heights with a straight line.
asks: How is the trapezium rule different from rectangles?
Should I use a straight line or a single point?

faq.q: When is the midpoint rule best to use?
faq.a: The midpoint rule often gives a very good estimate. It uses the height at the exact middle of the interval.
asks: Is the midpoint rule always accurate?
What is the best point to choose for the height?

faq.q: If the function is decreasing, which estimate is smaller?
faq.a: If the function is decreasing, the right endpoint will give an underestimate. The left endpoint will give an overestimate.
asks: Which estimate is smaller when the graph goes down?
Does the direction of the curve matter?

faq.q: Does the number of strips change the answer a lot?
faq.a: As you use more and more strips, the estimate gets closer to the true area. This is the goal of integration.
asks: What happens if I use many strips?
How close does it get to the real value?

faq.q: Can I use this method for any shape?
faq.a: These methods work best for finding the area under a curve. They approximate the area between the curve and the x-axis.
asks: What kind of area can I calculate?

facts: Riemann sums approximate area using rectangles.
The trapezium rule approximates area using trapezoids.
If a function is increasing, the right endpoint height overestimates the area.
The width of each strip is often denoted by delta x.

quiz.say: A function is rising steeply. Using the right endpoint height for a rectangle will result in:
quiz.why: When the function is going up, the right point is higher than the average height.

wrong.0: This is wrong because the relationship between increase and estimate is clear.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you think the right side is always lower.
wrong.3: This is wrong because Riemann sums are only approximations.

quiz.say: To find the area using the trapezium rule, what do you calculate for each strip?
quiz.why: The area of a trapezoid is found by averaging the two side heights and multiplying by the width.

wrong.0: This only calculates the area of a single rectangle.
wrong.1: Squaring the height is not part of the standard formula.
wrong.2: You must multiply by the width, not just add the heights.

quiz.say: If you increase the number of strips used for approximation, the total area calculated will:
quiz.show: Get closer to the true area

options.show: Get closer to the true area
options.say: Get closer to the true area

quiz.why: More strips mean the tops are cut into smaller segments, reducing the error.

wrong.0: While the number changes, the trend is towards accuracy, not just bigger numbers.
wrong.1: The approximation improves, so the value must change unless the function is linear.
wrong.2: The result could become an overestimate or an underestimate depending on the function's shape.
